newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian politicians voice fears for Albania force.
newsitem.headline: Italian politicians voice fears for Albania force.

text.p: Politicians expressed concern on Monday about the reception a planned Italian-led force to Albania would receive after scores of refugees drowned when their boat collided with an Italian navy ship last week.

Far-right parliamentary deputy Alessandra Mussolini, grand-daughter of the late Italian dictator whose troops occupied the Balkan country in 1939, called for the mission to be delayed until the situation calmed.

"Now, more than ever, it is not possible to send our soldiers to Albania when we must first mend diplomatic relations between our countries," she said. "Unless we want to send so many young people to be massacred."
Luigi Manconi, spokesman of the small Greens party, also called for Rome's participation to be re-assessed.

The government has insisted that the tragedy in the Adriatic, which Tirana says killed at least 83 people, makes the mission ever more urgent to stem a tide of refugees to Italy and bring some order to the impoverished Balkan state.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi said at the weekend he hoped the operation could start as soon as possible but politicians agreed the task had become tougher.

"It will certainly make our mission in Albania more difficult because many Albanians will undoubtedly have negative feelings against us," centre-right opposition leader Silvio Berlusconi said in the southern port of Brindisi on Sunday.
The small Albanian harbour patrol vessel crowded with refugees from the southern Albanian port of Vlore capsized and sank after colliding with a navy ship trying to turn it away.
Pandeli Pasko, the Albanian ambassador to Italy, told Italy's Channel 5 television he had compiled an updated list of people presumed dead and the total was 83.
Four bodies were recovered on Friday and 34 people rescued. Italy has ruled out finding anyone else alive.

The multinational force is due to secure Vlore, the northern port of Durres and Tirana airport for supplies, running short after the unrest. Albania's crisis was sparked by protests at the failure of savings schemes since late 1996.
About 7,000 people protested in Vlore on Sunday with some demonstrators making death threats against Italy.
Italian ships have been ordered by Rome to intercept Albanian boats heading for Italy and force them to turn back.

Berlusconi said the government must change its policies. "This blockade (must) be suspended absolutely because it is hard to see where it is leading us to," Forza Italia leader Berlusconi said, his voice shaking with emotion.
Junior Foreign Minister Piero Fassino countered that politicians must not exploit the tragedy.

"It is truly alarming that Berlusconi should go and cry in Brindisi when a large number of Forza Italia members have in recent days constantly accused the government of being too benevolent and permissive," he said.

"And it is even more alarming that a section of the political class should abandon themselves to this sort of exploitation at a time when thousands of our boys are leaving for Albania on a humanitarian mission of peace.

"This all risks creating a hostile climate around our men," Fassino said. "What happened in the Straits of Otranto cannot hide the fact that Italy has given shelter in a civilised fashion to almost 13,000 Albanians in just a few days."
Grieving survivors of Albania's worst maritime disaster since World War Two demanded action from Rome. "We want the truth," one man told RAI television.
Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini and Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta were expected to address the upper house of parliament on the situation on Tuesday.
